entries.test: Public funding records and Doublespeed's advertising would establish whether Andreessen Horowitz backs the company and whether it markets the described large-scale, human-mimicking account automation.
entries.note: The jointly authored essay asserts the claim in its own voice; the advertising quotations are supporting evidence.

entries.test: Public experiments or documented campaigns could establish whether duplicative, crawler-targeted swarm content contaminates model training data and influences resulting outputs.
entries.note: “Can” describes a testable attack capability here, rather than a probabilistic prediction.
“Ban our way out” specifies neither the bans considered nor what degree of threat reduction would count as success.

entries.test: Public deployment results or adversarial trials of verified-yet-anonymous proof-of-human requirements would show the technical feasibility and financial cost of secretly operating ten thousand accounts for high-reach interactions.
entries.note: The forecast depends on implementing the specified credential requirement and gives no deadline.
The proposition faithfully extracts the recommendation. The preceding access restriction is its rationale, rather than a stated conditional antecedent.

entries.test: Public attack demonstrations and platform studies could establish whether cheap coordinated accounts and rapidly fabricated identities enable coordinated manipulation of public discussion.
entries.note: The plain reading is that low costs and rapid impersonation enable attacks; “pennies” and “moments” are illustrative rather than exact thresholds.
